article_blocks.text: Strain Type: 60% Indica / 40% Sativa
Genetics: Exodus Cheese × Querkle
Breeder: Subcool / TGA Genetics
THC Content: 26%
CBD Content: N/A
Terpene Profile: Myrcene
Primary Flavors: Grape, sour cheese, cherry, lavender
Flowering Time (Indoor): 8–9 weeks
Outdoor Harvest Time: late September into October
Indoor Yield: Heavy
Outdoor Yield: High
Grow Difficulty: Easy to intermediate

Some marijuana strains make sense the instant their name is spoken, and Cheese Quake is one of them. The aroma can seem almost contradictory at first—ripe purple grapes and cherries colliding with sour, fermented Cheese funk—but curing brings those extremes together into something resembling a savory fruit pastry. Beneath that unconventional flavor sits a surprisingly forceful high.

The experience begins around the head with an unmistakable tingling cerebral surge before spreading into an energetic but increasingly substantial body stone. Add vigorous growth, purple coloration in some phenotypes, hard resinous flowers, and heavy production, and this weed becomes much more than a novelty cross. It represents Subcool’s terpene-focused approach to cannabis breeding particularly well: start with two highly recognizable parents and create something that tastes unlike either one on its own.
Genetics and Lineage

The verified lineage is Exodus Cheese × Querkle. Subcool described acquiring the Exodus Cheese cutting after encountering the cultivar during travels in the United Kingdom. Fascinated by its unusual pungency, he eventually paired the female with a Querkle male from his TGA breeding program. Querkle itself combines Purple Urkle and Space Queen , giving Cheese Quake a deeper genetic background that includes grape-heavy purple cannabis on one side and the energetic, resin-oriented Space Queen family on the other.

Exodus Cheese supplies the unmistakable sour funk. Rather than smelling literally like dairy cheese, the famous clone produces a penetrating fermented, musky aroma that became associated with the Cheese name because ordinary fruit, Skunk, and earth descriptions never quite captured it. Querkle pulls the offspring in a darker direction, contributing purple pigmentation and the grape-and-lavender qualities inherited from Purple Urkle. Space Queen adds additional vigor, resin production, and brighter fruit characteristics to the equation. Subcool specifically valued the way Purple Urkle’s grape-lavender profile interacted with the unusual smell of the Cheese mother.

Phenotypic variation is therefore part of the cultivar rather than a flaw. Cheese-dominant plants can lean pungent, sour, and funky, while Querkle-dominant selections often become sweeter, darker, and more obviously grape-oriented. The visual differences can be equally apparent, with some plants developing purple foliage and rounded flowers. What remains fairly consistent is the combination of dense bud formation, significant resin, vigorous growth, and an effect that occupies both the cerebral and physical sides of the cannabis experience.
Effects and Experience

Cheese Quake does not ease gently into the background. Subcool described the opening as a head-tingling initial buzz, and his original smoke test documented a sensation beginning around the back and top of the head before developing into a strong creeping high. That first phase can feel euphoric, mentally animated, and somewhat unusual in its intensity. Thoughts may become more associative, conversation more entertaining, and sensory details easier to focus on.

The body component develops soon afterward, but it does not necessarily resemble the immediate lethargy of a heavy nighttime indica. Instead, physical relaxation can coexist with an almost energetic internal buzz. That contrast is one of the strain’s most interesting qualities. Moderate consumption may leave someone relaxed yet engaged, while stronger servings can become considerably more disorienting and impairing. Subcool himself remarked that the potency surprised experienced consumers, which is why dose should be judged according to the specific flower rather than the strain’s playful flavor.

A standardized original THC percentage was not established during Subcool’s initial evaluation, so modern figures attached to the name should not be treated as universal. Cannabis chemistry varies with phenotype, growing environment, harvest timing, and testing method. THC can affect judgment, perception, memory, emotions, and coordination, and higher exposure may produce anxiety, fear, or panic in some people.
Medical Benefits

Cheese Quake was bred during an era when Subcool worked extensively with medical marijuana patients, and pain relief figured prominently in his evaluation of the cultivar. In his original report, he considered the cross more effective for his own pain than either parent and particularly valued the possibility of strong physical relief without the immediate drowsiness associated with some potent indica varieties. These observations provide useful historical context, but they should not be interpreted as clinical evidence that this particular strain treats pain or another medical condition.

Cannabis research more broadly does provide some evidence relevant to pain. The National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health reports that studies of cannabis and cannabinoids for chronic pain have found small benefits overall, although the difference compared with placebo can be modest and side effects must also be considered. That evidence applies to cannabis or cannabinoid preparations generally rather than Cheese Quake specifically.

The cultivar’s combination of euphoria and physical relaxation may also appeal to medical consumers looking to unwind without becoming instantly sleepy. Still, high-THC marijuana can produce dizziness, cognitive impairment, anxiety, and unwanted sedation as dose increases. Anyone considering cannabis for persistent pain or another diagnosed condition should evaluate cannabinoid dosage, personal tolerance, medication interactions, and professional healthcare advice rather than relying solely on strain reputation.
Flavor Profile and Aroma

Flavor is where Cheese Quake earns its place among Subcool’s more memorable creations. He famously compared the combination to a grape cheese Danish, an unusual but remarkably useful description of how the two parental profiles interact. Querkle-dominant plants can release grape, cherry, lavender, and musty purple-fruit notes, while Cheese-dominant phenotypes emphasize sourness and penetrating fermented funk.

The inhale can begin surprisingly sweet. Grape and dark fruit lead in some examples, sometimes joined by cherry before the sharper Cheese component develops. On the exhale, sourness, musk, spice, and resin tend to become stronger. Proper curing integrates these characteristics especially well, changing the aroma from a collection of competing smells into a layered mixture of fruit, pastry-like sweetness, and savory cannabis funk. Subcool noted that the complexity became more pronounced after curing.

Myrcene has been identified as an important component of the cultivar’s terpene expression, although exact terpene ratios should always be taken from the laboratory analysis of the particular harvest. Phenotype matters considerably here: one plant may emphasize grape and lavender, while another pushes Cheese, sour fruit, and musk to the foreground.
Growing Information

Cheese Quake earned Subcool’s recommendation partly because it is relatively straightforward to cultivate. The plants show strong seedling vigor and fast vegetative development without demanding unusual feeding or training methods. In Subcool’s documented grow, seedlings were maintained for roughly 45 days before flowering, and the selected females developed rapidly after being transplanted into five-gallon containers. They grew successfully in an organic soil-based system with comparatively simple feeding.

Plant structure changes dramatically according to training. Left untopped, Cheese Quake can develop the familiar central-leader or Christmas-tree shape, while topping encourages a wider, heavily branched bush. Indoor examples tend to stay relatively stocky when flowered early, making the strain compatible with Sea of Green arrangements. Given additional vegetative time outdoors, plants can exceed six feet. The cultivar is regarded as a heavy producer, and purple foliage may emerge toward maturity in Querkle-influenced phenotypes.

Flowering generally takes eight to nine weeks. Subcool harvested two original test females at 58 and 61 days, with each producing about three ounces from a five-gallon container. Even lower flowers were described as dense and hard, suggesting useful production throughout the illuminated canopy rather than only at the main tops. Dense buds benefit from consistent airflow and controlled humidity late in bloom, particularly when growing large plants or tightly packed indoor gardens.
FAQ
Is Cheese Quake indica or sativa?
Cheese Quake is generally considered an indica-leaning hybrid, approximately 60% indica and 40% sativa. Its effects nevertheless combine pronounced cerebral stimulation with a substantial body stone.
What are the genetics of Cheese Quake?

The original lineage is Exodus Cheese × Querkle. Querkle itself comes from Purple Urkle × Space Queen, giving the cultivar its mixture of Cheese funk, grape sweetness, purple coloration, and resinous growth.
What does Cheese Quake taste like?

Expect a complex combination of grape, sour Cheese, cherry, lavender, musk, and sweet pastry-like flavors. Different phenotypes may lean more heavily toward either the grape-rich Querkle side or the pungent Cheese parent.
How long does Cheese Quake take to flower?

Indoor flowering generally requires eight to nine weeks. Subcool harvested representative plants at 58 and 61 days, making roughly 55–65 days a practical working window depending on phenotype and environment.
Is Cheese Quake easy to grow?

Yes. Subcool specifically recommended the cultivar to home growers because of its vigor, uncomplicated cultivation, attractive appearance, and heavy production. It can be grown untopped, trained into a bush, or flowered early in a Sea of Green arrangement.
Final Thoughts on Cheese Quake

Cheese Quake demonstrates why Subcool’s breeding work became so influential among growers interested in flavor rather than potency alone. Exodus Cheese contributes unmistakable sour funk, while Querkle layers grape, lavender, purple coloration, and a sweeter fruit character over the top. Instead of one parent overwhelming the other, the offspring creates a new sensory identity—part fruit, part fermented Cheese, and part sweet pastry.

The plant backs that unusual flavor with practical traits. Vigorous growth, heavy production, dense flowers, an eight-to-nine-week bloom, and flexible training make the weed approachable for home cultivation, while its euphoric cerebral onset and increasingly strong body stone give consumers a distinctly layered experience. Cheese Quake may have emerged before the modern obsession with dessert strains, but its grape-and-Cheese complexity feels surprisingly contemporary. More importantly, it remains a clear example of what Subcool did particularly well: combining recognizable cannabis families in ways that produced flavors and effects neither parent could deliver alone.
